name: Cook Islands
summary_text: The Cook Islands are self-governing in free association with New Zealand. New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to Cook Islanders, while local criminal law governs conduct on the islands.  Sections 154 and 155 of the Cook Islands Crimes Act 1969 criminalised sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male. Consent was explicitly not a defence. Reported maximum terms differ across sources: the 2017 coverage of the draft reform gives seven years for sex between men and five years for an indecent act, while later reporting on the repeal cites exposure of up to ten years for indecent acts between males. All sources agree the offences were never enforced in living memory.  Parliament voted on Friday 14 April 2023 to strike the provisions from the Crimes Act through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023. A note attached to the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands, and the same bill added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault.  Same-sex marriage remains prohibited. The Marriage Amendment Act 2000 defines marriage as between a man and a woman, so a foreign same-sex marriage is not recognised locally and a trans visitor in a same-sex relationship has no spousal standing.  The repeal followed a protracted legislative path. A 2017 select committee recommended removing sections 154 and 155, and the provisions were struck from the draft Crimes Bill, which was drafted with New Zealand assistance; MPs subsequently backtracked. In October 2020 deferral continued when members again pushed the bill's report back, this time by three months, before the 2023 passage.

name: Comoros
summary_text: Both male and female same-sex sexual acts are criminal under national law in Comoros. Article 300 of the 2020 Penal Code punishes any act of a sexual nature contrary to morality or unnatural with six months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 francs, equivalent to US$240 to US$720. Other sources report different maxima for the same conduct. The Human Dignity Trust profile gives up to three years imprisonment. A December 2024 press report cites Article 318 as carrying up to five years. The prior 1982 Penal Code provided up to five years and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs.  Enforcement against same-sex intimacy is documented. In 2022 a man was prosecuted and imprisoned after a sexual video showing him with another man was leaked online, described as the first prosecution of consensual adult same-sex activity under the 2020 Code. In June 2024 two women were detained after asking an imam to marry them. The request was not proven in court. The women stated they had previously engaged in sexual activity together. On 12 December 2024 a court convicted both of homosexuality and sentenced them to five and six months respectively, releasing them because detention since June exceeded the sentences. Reuters reported their release following the verdict.  A United States government human-rights report for 2023 stated that authorities reported no arrests or prosecutions for same-sex conduct that year and did not actively enforce the law. Police were reported not to incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ persons, with no such violence reported in that year. This account predates the June to December 2024 detention and conviction.  Transgender persons are not permitted to change gender markers. No law protects against discrimination based on gender identity. The 2012 Labor Code provides no protections for LGBTQ persons. No general non-discrimination law exists.  Same-sex couples have no legal recognition. The Family Code defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman.
